Sixth grade science · Unit 15

Data & Statistics

Science runs on numbers, but a pile of numbers says nothing until you summarize and graph it. This unit teaches the tools every other unit leans on: the center of a data set (mean, median, mode), its spread, the right graph for the job, and how sample size changes how much you can trust a result. It can be taught any time after Unit 0.

Where we left off: Unit 0 taught fair tests and repeated trials. This unit is the next step: once you have several measurements, how do you describe them honestly? Later units, like climate (Unit 8.11) and health evidence (Unit 7.11), use these tools.

In this unit

  1. Center
  2. Spread

Concept 1 · Center

Mean, median and mode

The mean is the sum divided by the count, the median is the middle value when the data are in order, and the mode is the most common value. An outlier, a value far from the rest, drags the mean a lot and the median only a little.

Analogy

A seesaw and a line

The mean is the balance point of a seesaw loaded with your data. The median is the middle value when the numbers are lined up in order.

Step 1. Press Start: 2, 3, 3, 4. Each block is one data value, sitting at its spot on the number line. The seesaw is balanced on a triangle.

Step 2. Slide the triangle left and right. The seesaw tips toward the heavier side. Find the spot where it sits perfectly level. That spot is the mean.

Step 3. Press Add the 18. One far-away block now tips the seesaw. Slide the triangle until it is level again: the balance point moved a long way toward the 18. You can also tap above the number line to add your own blocks.

The median, same numbers: line the values up from smallest to largest and take the one in the middle (if there are two in the middle, take the number halfway between them).

Where it breaks: a real seesaw also depends on how heavy each person is; here every block weighs the same.

Try it

Add an outlier

Predict. You have a set of plant heights. If one plant is suddenly 38 cm tall, will the mean change a lot, a little, or not at all? What about the median?

Do. Pick a data set (try Plant heights first). Look at where the mean and median are marked on the dot plot. Then press Add an outlier and look again. Repeat with the bean seeds and test times.

Notice. In the plant-height data the median stays at 17 cm, but the mean jumps from about 17.2 to 18.6 cm when the 38 cm plant is added. The mean chases the outlier; the median hardly moves. Same effect in all three data sets.

Why it matters. One odd value can make an average misleading. That is why news reports use the median for house prices and incomes, and why scientists check an odd value before deciding whether it is a mistake or something real.

Data

Which to use

MeasureBest forWatch out for
MeanData without extreme values; uses every numberPulled by outliers
MedianSkewed data or outliers, like house pricesIgnores how far extremes are
ModeCategories or repeated values, like shoe sizeMay not exist or may not be unique
Real world

Mean or median?

0 of 5 correct

Concept 2 · Spread

Two sets can share a mean and still differ

Spread tells how far values are from each other. The range is largest minus smallest. The interquartile range (IQR) is the width of the middle half. The mean absolute deviation (MAD) is the average distance from the mean. Small spread means measurements agree; large spread means more variation or less careful measuring.

Analogy

Archery targets

Two archers can average the center of the target. One lands all arrows close together and the other scatters them. The mean is the same; the spread is not.

Try it

Compare two plant groups

Predict. Group A and Group B each have eight plants. Do you think they have the same average height? Which group is easier to predict?

Do. Press Group A, then Group B, then Both. Read the mean, MAD (mean absolute deviation), and range for each.

Notice. Both groups have the same mean of 20 cm, but Group A runs only from 17 to 23 cm (range 6) while Group B runs from 10 to 30 cm (range 20). B has a much larger MAD too. The mean alone would never tell you that.

Why it matters. A mean without a spread hides half of the story. In an experiment, small spread means your measurements agree. Large spread means more variation, or less careful measuring, so you should trust the average less.

Data

Computing spread by hand

StepExample: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12
Mean(4+6+8+10+12)/5 = 8
Distances from mean4, 2, 0, 2, 4
MAD(4+2+0+2+4)/5 = 2.4
Range12 - 4 = 8
Median8; lower half 4, 6 (median 5), upper half 10, 12 (median 11); IQR = 11 - 5 = 6

Quartiles are found by splitting at the median and taking the median of each half.

Real world

Why spread matters in science

When you time a falling ball five times and get 0.62, 0.63, 0.61, 0.62, 0.64 seconds, the spread is small: the measurement is reliable. If you get 0.4, 0.9, 0.6, 1.1, 0.5, you cannot trust the mean to be close to the truth.

The two sets from the paragraph above. Their means are not equal (0.62 and 0.70 seconds), but the point is the spread: the sloppy set’s mean could be a long way from the true time.

Concept 3 · Choosing a graph

The question decides the graph

Pick a graph by what you want to show: a bar graph compares categories, a histogram shows how a number is distributed in bins, a line graph shows change over time, a scatter plot shows how two numbers relate, and a dot plot shows every value in a small set. A graph can mislead if its axis is trimmed or its scale is stretched.

Analogy

Tools in a toolbox

A hammer is great for nails and bad for screws. No graph is best for every job.

Try it

Honest or trimmed axis?

Predict. Two bars, 92 and 96. Does one look twice as big as the other? Predict how different they will look when the axis starts at 0 versus at 90.

Do. Press Starts at 0 (honest), then Starts at 90 (trimmed). Compare the heights of the two bars in each picture and read the sentence below.

Notice. With a trimmed axis the bar for 96 looks about three times as tall as the bar for 92, even though the values differ by only 4%. With the axis starting at 0, the bars look nearly equal, which is the truth.

Why it matters. Bar length should match the amount. When a graph’s axis starts above zero, it makes small differences look huge. Check the axis before you believe a graph, and start your own bar graphs at zero.

Data

Graph chooser

You want to showUseExample
Compare amounts in categoriesBar graphRainfall in four cities
Show how data spread across rangesHistogramHeights of 30 students in 5 cm bins
Show change over timeLine graphDaily temperature for a month
Show if two numbers are relatedScatter plotRamp height versus roll distance
Show every value in a small setDot plotFive plant heights

Concept 4 · Samples and trials

More trials mean more trust

A sample is the part you measure. A larger, random sample usually gives a result closer to the truth. Repeating a test and averaging smooths out luck. If a value looks like a mistake, find out why before dropping it; never delete numbers just because they are inconvenient.

Analogy

Tasting a soup

One spoonful from a well-stirred pot tells you about the pot. One spoonful from the top, before stirring, might not. A random, well-mixed sample represents the whole.

Try it

Flip a coin many times

Predict. A fair coin should land heads half the time. If you flip it 10 times in one run, will you always get exactly 5 heads? Which will be closer to 50%: runs of 10 flips or runs of 1,000?

Do. Press 10 flips and look at the 12 runs as dots. Press New runs a couple of times to see more. Then do 100 flips and 1,000 flips.

Notice. With 10 flips the runs are all over the place (20% to 80% heads is normal). With 100 they bunch near 50%, and with 1,000 they sit in a narrow band around 50%. The true share is still 50% every time; the sample size is what changes.

Why it matters. More trials means you can trust the result more. One run of 10 flips can fool you, but many flips shows the truth. This is why experiments need repeated trials and surveys need big samples.

Data

What sample size does

Flips per runTypical range for share of heads (about 95% of runs)
1020% to 80%
10040% to 60%
1,00047% to 53%
10,00049% to 51%

The range shrinks as the sample size grows, about in proportion to one over the square root of the number of flips. A fair coin has a true share of 50%.

Real world

Real-world samples

QuestionWeak sampleBetter sample
Do students like the lunch menu?Ask three friendsAsk a random 10% of each grade
Does fertilizer help plants?One pot eachTen pots each, same soil and light
Is the creek polluted?One scoop on one daySeveral spots, several days

Check yourself

Can you explain it?

Two classes tested the same paper airplane. Class A threw it 5 times (mean 8.2 m, range 3 m). Class B threw it 50 times (mean 7.6 m, range 5 m). Which result do you trust more, and what would you do next?

Show a model answer

Class B's mean rests on 10 times as many throws, so it is more reliable even though its range is larger (more throws means more chances for extreme throws). I would repeat the test, check that both classes threw the same way, and look at a graph of all the throws before deciding which mean to use.

0 of 6 correct

Words to know

mean
The sum of the values divided by how many there are.
median
The middle value of a list in order.
mode
The most common value.
outlier
A value far from the others.
range
Largest value minus smallest.
interquartile range
The width of the middle half of the data.
sample
The part of a group you actually measure.
mean absolute deviation
The average distance of the values from the mean.
Tutor notes: hands-on kit, misconceptions, pacing

Kit: graph paper, rulers, coins, a stopwatch, bean seeds or paper airplanes, a spreadsheet if available.

  • Concept 1: Measure the class's hand spans; find mean, median and mode; add the teacher as an outlier (or a made-up data point) and recompute.
  • Concept 2: Time a falling object 10 times; compute range and MAD.
  • Concept 3: Graph the same data as a bar graph with and without a trimmed axis.
  • Concept 4: Flip a coin 10 times, then pool the class for 300 flips.

Common misconceptions:

  • "The mean is always the best average." Not with outliers.
  • "A bigger range always means worse data." More trials make the range larger, even when the data are fine.
  • "If heads came up 7 times in 10, the coin is unfair." Small samples vary.
  • "Delete outliers." Check first.

Pacing: about four 30-minute sessions. Method link: pair with Unit 0 on repeated trials.
